title: Deserts and Grasslands of the World

cards.h: Dry lands and open plains cover a third of the earth
cards.b:
Deserts cover about a third of land, and grasslands feed the world. UPSC asks about their causes, local names, the rain shadow, desertification and wheat belts. Combine them with the biomes and climate lessons.

Both biomes appear in the prelims every few years, often through a map, a local name or a cause of desert formation, so keep the lists below ready.

Causes: (1) subtropical highs with sinking air (Sahara, Arabian, Thar, Australian). (2) Rain shadow (Patagonia, Great Basin, Ladakh). (3) Cold offshore currents that cool air and stop rain (Atacama with the Humboldt, Namib with the Benguela, Western Australian with the West Australian current). (4) Continentality (Gobi, Taklamakan).

Sahara (about 9 million sq km, largest hot desert), Arabian, Thar, Kalahari, Namib (oldest), Great Australian (Gibson, Great Sandy, Great Victoria), Sonoran and Mojave, Atacama (the driest non-polar place, some stations with almost no rain). Landforms: erg (sand sea), reg (stony), hamada (rocky), wadi (dry river bed), oasis, playa.

Gobi (China and Mongolia), Taklamakan, Patagonia, Great Basin, Ladakh, Turkestan. They have rain under 25-50 cm and cold winters. Antarctica is a polar desert, the largest desert on Earth. Many cold deserts lie in the rain shadow of high ranges.

Oases form where the water table meets the surface, and the date palm is the key crop. Salt crust and wind erosion are the two worst enemies of oasis farming.

Plants: xerophytes with deep roots or water-storing stems. Animals: camels, fennec foxes, lizards, many nocturnal. People: nomads (Bedouin of Arabia, Tuareg of the Sahara, Bishnoi and Rabari in the Thar), oasis farming, and oil economies such as Saudi Arabia. The Thar is the most densely populated desert in the world.

Prairies (North America), Pampas (Argentina, Uruguay), Steppes (Eurasia), Veld (South Africa), Downs (Australia, New Zealand), Canterbury (New Zealand). Rain 25-75 cm, chernozem and prairie soils. Very fertile, so most have been turned into wheat and maize farms, or cattle ranches. They have few trees because of the dry spells, fire and grazing.

Africa's savanna (the Serengeti, Masai Mara), Llanos (Orinoco, Venezuela), Campos (Brazil), the Australian tropical grasslands. Wet summer, dry winter. Grass with scattered acacia and baobab. Wildlife: elephant, lion, zebra, giraffe. Threats: poaching, farming, drought. Hosts the great wildebeest migration.

The Serengeti hosts one of the largest land animal migrations, with over a million wildebeest following the rains each year between Tanzania and Kenya.

Land degradation in dry areas from climate and human pressure: overgrazing, deforestation, bad irrigation. The Sahel, south of the Sahara, is the textbook case after the 1970s droughts. The UN Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD) was adopted in 1994 (in force 1996). The Great Green Wall of Africa aims to restore 100 million hectares. China's 'Great Green Wall' (Three-North shelterbelt) aims to halt the Gobi's advance.

Nearly 30 percent of India's land is degraded, about 97 million hectares (ISRO atlas 2021). India hosted the UNCCD COP14 (2019, Greater Noida) and pledged to restore 26 million hectares by 2030. Rajasthan's Indira Gandhi canal brought irrigation to the Thar. The Cold Desert in Ladakh and Spiti is a biosphere reserve.

Likely questions: 'Why are deserts found on the west coasts of continents?', 'Desertification: causes and control', 'Compare prairies and savanna'.

  • For west-coast deserts: subtropical highs plus cold currents plus trade winds blowing offshore.
  • For control: afforestation, drip irrigation, community management.
  • Name the local grassland names with their continents.
